place.zh: 沂中医 · 解剖实验室 · 古籍部
place.en: Yizhong · the anatomy lab · the rare-books room

setup.zh: 默写十二正经交了白卷；解剖台上看见了膈肌；图书馆负一层，一个记错朝代的老太太说：先吐。
setup.en: A blank sheet for the twelve meridians; the diaphragm on the dissecting table; and in the library basement an old woman who gets her dynasties wrong says: out first.

recap.zh: 解剖台上的膈肌，葛奶奶的《养性延命录》，门边那一函《九鼎真人手札》：喘不上来，先吐。
recap.en: The diaphragm on the table, Granny Ge's old book and the thick journal by the door: when you can't get breath, breathe out first.

zh: 白卷上只剩两个字：沈芒。
膈肌，像一张绷紧的鼓皮。
en: Only two characters left on the blank sheet: his name.
The diaphragm, like a drumskin pulled tight.

story.zh:
开课头一天，一食堂二楼，马小宝的餐盘「咣」地落在他对面：「你来球队图什么，我看出来了，她没看出来——她看什么都是数。十月十七试训，你要是过不了，」他笑得很和气，「我替你跟她说。」

下午解剖课绪论，老师在黑板上画了一个人，从外往里一层一层地标：皮肤，浅筋膜，深筋膜，肌肉，血管神经，骨头。沈芒举起手：「老师，那经络在第几层？」后排有人「噗」地笑出了声。那位说话很轻的女老师没有笑，想了想：「解剖学到今天，没有找到经络这样一种单独的结构。」她把手里的骨盆模型放下，又道：「两千多年前没有解剖刀，古人只有手。按这儿，酸麻往那儿走；扎这儿，那儿的疼轻了；摸脉，一跳一跳，连着。一处一处记下来，连成线——长沙马王堆出土的帛书上，还只有十一条，后来才凑成十二条，配一年十二个月。」她顿了顿，「这几十年，有人顺着线切开看，有人往穴位里打同位素，有人说找着了一种细管子，别人照着再做，做不出来。切开了，是血管、神经、筋膜，各走各的。」她拿粉笔在黑板上画了一个省的轮廓：「经络像地图上这条省界。地上挖不出这条线，可你过了界，口音就变了。」

找不着，默写照样要默。礼拜四上午，针灸推拿学导论，严老师在黑板上写了一行，粉笔敲得笃笃响：

「经脉者，所以能决死生，处百病，调虚实，不可不通。」

「收书，默写十二正经。」他背着手一排一排地走，「去年有人抄在胳膊上。」

沈芒左胳膊里侧，细笔抄着十二行。他把手揣进桌肚，拿唾沫使劲搓，搓完一看，十二行糊成了一片蓝。

严老师翻到一张，停住，举起来：「沈芒。白卷。」后排有人笑。「十二条都背不下来的，可以早点想想，是不是走错了门。」

卷子发回来，只剩右上角两个字：沈芒。他叠了两叠，塞进兜里最深处。

那夜他没背书。他把书摊在桌上，翻到那张小人图，站到宿舍正中，两只胳膊举过头顶——图上那个小人，就是这么举着的。

他从胸口找起：锁骨底下一寸，手太阴肺经从这儿出来，顺着胳膊里侧往上走，走到大拇指尖。大拇指挨着食指，手阳明大肠经接住了，顺着胳膊外侧往下，翻过肩膀，落到鼻子旁边。鼻子旁边，足阳明胃经接过去，从脸上往下，过胸，过肚子，过膝盖前头，落到第二个脚趾。第二个脚趾挨着大脚趾，足太阴脾经接住，又顺着腿里侧往上，回到了胸口。

他的手停在胸口，愣住了。回来了。

他接着比第二圈：胸口出来，到小指；小指翻到手背，下来到耳朵前头；眼角里头起，翻过头顶，顺着后背一路往下，到小脚趾；脚底板再往上，又回到胸口——这一圈，全走在背后。第三圈：胸口到中指；无名指下来，到眉梢；眼角外头起，顺着身子两侧往下，到第四个脚趾；大脚趾再往上，回到胸口，又接上了肺经。

他站在那儿，两只胳膊还举着，忽然全明白了。举着手，阴经全往上走，阳经全往下走；手指尖上、脚趾尖上，阴阳换手；脸上，阳经跟阳经换手；胸口里，阴经跟阴经换手。哪里是十二条各管各的线——是一条，绕着人跑三圈：头一圈走前面，第二圈走后面，第三圈走两边。像一班接力的人，跑一圈又回来，把棒子交到下一个人手里。

眼镜在对面床上，把眼镜往上一推：「……你再比一遍，我录下来。」

他闭上眼睛，又比了一遍，一条没错。第二天上午重默，过了。

九月二十一日，解剖实验室。台脚边一张塑封卡片：「刘桂芝，女，七十九岁。生前是小学老师。她留了一句话：让孩子们别怕，好好学。」四十个人弯下腰去，沈芒弯得最深，深到看见了自己的鞋尖。

那位说话很轻的女老师管她叫「大体老师」：「这是你们头一位老师，一句话不说，教你们一学期。」规矩也是她当场讲的：不许拍照，不许说笑；白布只揭开今天要看的那一块，别处盖好；切下来的，哪怕指甲盖大一小片，也要放回原处——学期末，大体老师要囫囵个儿地送去火化，每年清明，学校还给她们开追思会。福尔马林的味儿冲得人眼睛发酸，两层口罩也挡不住；第一节课下来，好几个人一个礼拜没吃肉。

老师拿镊子指着肺底下横着的一大片肉，薄薄的，往上拱：「膈肌。你吸气，主要是它在干活。」轮到他拿指头按一按，像一张绷紧的鼓皮。他想起那一千米：肩膀一耸一耸，脖子上的筋鼓着，肚子从头到尾一动没动。

傍晚他一个人去体育场，要拿肚子喘。阿禾从跑道边上过，站住了：「反了。你一吸，肚子往里收。」他低头一看，可不是，胸口一挺，像一只受了惊的鸽子。

「人一慌，就这么喘，又浅又快。」阿禾道，「每口气总有一截堵在喉咙、气管里，到不了肺，下一口又原样吐出来——跟挤公交一样，门口那一截人永远进不了车厢。喘得越浅越快，白喘得越多。你那天第四百米，一半是白喘。」

「那怎么办？」

「门口那截人，先下车。」她合上本子走了。

九月二十二日下午，他在图书馆负一层一道灰色防火门前站了二十分钟。门里出来一个老太太，蓝布套袖，老花镜挂在链子上。

「奶奶，有没有那种……一般人看不懂、看懂了就特别厉害的书？」

「有。」老太太道，「字典。」

她姓葛，说葛洪是她们老葛家的，五百年前是一家。她捧出一函线装书：「陶弘景，《养性延命录》。唐朝的。」竖排繁体，一页全讲怎么往外出气。他认到一句，停住了：

「凡人极者，则多嘘呬。」

人累到了头，就多嘘、多呬。他蹲在跑道边上一口一口往外吐的，可不就是这个。原来一千五百年前，就有人看见过他。

函套里夹着一张发黄的借阅卡。一九八几年，一个名字连着登了十几格，字写得很小，很急，后来洇了水，认不出了；再往下，一格也没有。他在头一个空格里写下「沈芒，2026.9.22」，看着上头那个名字，心里动了一下。

葛奶奶把函套合上，像是顺嘴：「这一函讲的，就是先吐。吐干净了，它自己就进来了。」

门口那截人，先下车。他站在那儿，半天没动。

取包的时候，他蹲到门边那架矮书架前头。最底层横着一函旧书，函套磨得发白，签条掉了；解开，里头八册，每册都有两指厚，书脊上只有墨笔写的「一」到「八」。他抽出头一册，扉页上六个毛笔字：《九鼎真人手札》。翻开，头一行：

「余少时，人呼为漏勺。」

沈芒「噗」地笑出了声。一个真人，开口先管自己叫漏勺——这老头有意思。往下翻，不是功法，是日记，一条一条，短得像记账：「十二岁，坠谷。谷底一狐，断尾，饿。分它半张饼。」「是冬，学吐纳。鹅毛日日飞。」隔了几页，单单一行：「修仙先修心。」

坠的哪道谷，哪来的狐狸，他看不明白；可一个人从十二岁记起，记了厚厚八册。他把头一册塞回函里，塞得跟原先一样。

那夜熄了灯，他仰面躺着，肚皮上压一本一千多页的《正常人体解剖学》。「呵——」长长吐干净，书往下沉；鼻子吸，书慢慢升上去。吐到第七口，肚子往下一瘪，底下跟着「噗——」一声，声音很小。沈芒心想：应该没人注意。老蔡在上铺躺不住了，「噌」地探下半个身子，捏着鼻子：「沈忙，你漏气了？」对床的眼镜「哈哈哈哈」笑得直拍床板，笑够了，才道：「我查了。陶弘景是南朝梁的，不是唐朝。葛洪也不是五百年前，是一千七百来年。」沈芒道：「朝代记错了。那一句，没错。」

九月二十三日，马小宝在草坪边蹲下来：「明天补测七个人。我赌你第七——倒数第一。赌一箱蛋白粉：你不是第七，箱子归你。」他拍拍沈芒的脸，「是第七，十月十七你也别来了，省得我当着她的面，替你说那句话。」
story.en:
The first day of classes, upstairs in Canteen One, Ma Xiaobao's tray landed with a clang across from him: "What you joined the team for, I can see; she can't — all she sees is numbers. Tryouts are October seventeenth. If you don't make it," he smiled very pleasantly, "I'll tell her for you."

In the afternoon, at the introductory anatomy lecture, the teacher drew a person on the board and labelled the layers from the outside in: skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia, muscle, vessels and nerves, bone. Shen Mang raised his hand. "Teacher — then which layer are the meridians in?" Someone in the back row snorted out loud. The soft-spoken woman teaching didn't laugh. She thought for a moment. "To this day anatomy has not found any separate structure like a meridian." She set down the pelvis model in her hands and went on: "Two thousand years ago there were no scalpels; people had only their hands. Press here, and an ache travels there; put a needle here, and the pain over there eases; feel the pulse, beat after beat, joined up. They wrote it down one spot at a time and joined the spots into lines — on the silk manuscripts dug up at Mawangdui in Changsha there are still only eleven; later they were made up to twelve, to match the twelve months of the year." She paused. "In the last few decades people have cut along the lines to look, injected isotopes into the points, and someone said he'd found a kind of fine duct — others did the same work and couldn't find it. Cut it open and it's blood vessels, nerves, fascia, each going its own way." With the chalk she drew the outline of a province on the board. "The meridians are like this provincial border on a map. You can't dig the line out of the ground — but cross it, and the accent changes."

Found or not, you still had to write them out from memory. Thursday morning, Introduction to Acupuncture and Tuina, Teacher Yan wrote a line on the blackboard, the chalk knocking tok-tok:

"The channels are what decide death and life, treat the hundred diseases, and regulate deficiency and excess; they must not be blocked."

"Books away. Write out the twelve regular channels." He walked the rows one by one, hands behind his back. "Last year someone copied them onto his arm."

On the inside of Shen Mang's left arm, in fine pen, were twelve lines. He shoved the arm under the desk and scrubbed hard with spit; when he looked, the twelve lines had blurred into one blue smear.

Teacher Yan turned to one paper, stopped, and held it up: "Shen Mang. Blank." Someone in the back row laughed. "Anyone who can't memorise twelve lines might think early about whether he's come in the wrong door."

When the paper came back, all that was left was two characters in the top right corner: Shen Mang. He folded it twice and pushed it into the deepest corner of his pocket. That night he didn't study the book. He opened it on the desk to the little figure, stood in the middle of the dorm, and raised both arms over his head — the little man in the picture held his arms just so.

He started at the chest: a thumb's width under the collarbone, the Lung channel of hand-taiyin comes out and runs up the inside of the arm to the tip of the thumb. The thumb sits beside the index finger, and the Large Intestine channel of hand-yangming takes over, running down the outside of the arm, over the shoulder, to beside the nose. Beside the nose the Stomach channel of foot-yangming takes it, down the face, down the chest, the belly, the front of the knee, to the second toe. The second toe sits beside the big toe, and the Spleen channel of foot-taiyin picks it up and runs up the inside of the leg — back to the chest.

His hand stopped on his chest. He froze. It had come back.

He went on with the second lap: out of the chest to the little finger; from the little finger over the back of the hand, down to the front of the ear; from the inner corner of the eye up over the crown, all the way down the back to the little toe; up from the sole of the foot, back to the chest — this lap ran entirely behind him. The third: chest to the middle finger; down from the ring finger to the end of the eyebrow; from the outer corner of the eye down the sides of the body to the fourth toe; up from the big toe, back to the chest, and joined the Lung channel again.

He stood there, arms still raised, and suddenly saw the whole of it. Arms up, every yin channel runs up and every yang channel runs down; at the fingertips and the toe tips, yin hands over to yang; on the face, yang hands to yang; in the chest, yin hands to yin. Not twelve lines each minding its own business — one line, running three laps round a person: the first lap down the front, the second down the back, the third down the sides. Like a relay team going round the lap and back again, putting the baton into the next hand.

Specs, on the bed opposite, pushed his glasses up. "…Do it again. I'm filming."

He closed his eyes and traced it again, not one wrong. The next morning he rewrote it and passed.

September the twenty-first, the anatomy lab. By the foot of the table, a laminated card: "Liu Guizhi, female, seventy-nine. A primary school teacher in life. She left one sentence: Tell the children not to be afraid, and to study well." Forty people bowed; Shen Mang bowed deepest, deep enough to see the tips of his own shoes.

The soft-spoken woman teacher called her "Teacher Body": "She is your first teacher. She won't say a word, and she'll teach you for a whole term." She gave the rules on the spot, too: no photographs, no joking; lift the white sheet only from the part you are studying today and keep the rest covered; whatever you cut away, even a sliver the size of a fingernail, goes back where it came from — at the end of term Teacher Body is sent for cremation whole, and every Qingming the school holds a memorial for them. The formalin stung the eyes; two masks couldn't keep it out. After the first class, quite a few of them didn't eat meat for a week.

With tweezers the teacher pointed to a broad sheet of muscle lying across beneath the lungs, thin, arching upward: "The diaphragm. When you breathe in, it does most of the work." When his turn came to press it with a finger, it was like a drumskin pulled tight. He thought of the thousand metres: shoulders heaving up and up, cords standing out on his neck, and his belly not moving once from start to finish.

At dusk he went to the stadium alone to try breathing with his belly. Ahe passed along the edge of the track and stopped: "Backwards. When you breathe in, your belly pulls in." He looked down — sure enough, his chest puffed out like a startled pigeon.

"When people panic, that's how they breathe, shallow and fast," said Ahe. "Every breath, a stretch of it is stuck in the throat and windpipe and never reaches the lungs, and the next breath pushes it straight back out — like a crowded bus: the people by the door never make it into the bus. The shallower and faster you breathe, the more of it's wasted. On your fourth hundred metres that day, half your breathing was wasted."

"So what do I do?"

"The people by the door get off first." She shut her notebook and left.

On the afternoon of September the twenty-second he stood for twenty minutes in front of a grey fire door on the library's lower basement level. Out of it came an old woman in blue cloth oversleeves, reading glasses hanging on a chain.

"Granny, do you have the kind of book... that ordinary people can't understand, but once you do, you're really something?"

"I do," said the old woman. "The dictionary."

Her name was Ge; she said Ge Hong belonged to their Ge family, they'd been one family five hundred years ago. She brought out a cased set of thread-bound volumes: "Tao Hongjing, *Records of Nourishing Nature and Prolonging Life*. Tang dynasty." Vertical lines, traditional characters, a whole page on nothing but how to breathe out. He made out one sentence and stopped:

"When a man is at his limit, he breathes out much with xu and with xi."

When people are worn out to the end, they breathe out more, with a xu and a xi. Squatting at the side of the track spitting out breath after breath — wasn't that exactly it? So fifteen hundred years ago someone had already seen him.

Tucked in the case was a yellowed borrowing card. In the nineteen-eighties one name filled a dozen or so rows in a row, written very small and very hurried, later smudged by water, illegible; below that, not a single entry. In the first empty row he wrote "Shen Mang, 2026.9.22," looked at the name above, and felt something stir.

Granny Ge closed the case and said, as if in passing: "That's what this whole case is about: out first. Once it's all out, it comes in by itself."

The people by the door get off first. He stood there and didn't move for a long time.

When he went for his bag, he crouched at the low bookcase by the door. Lying flat on the bottom shelf was a case of old books, its cloth worn pale, the label gone; he untied it, and inside were eight volumes, each two fingers thick, with nothing on the spines but a brushed numeral, one to eight. He drew out the first. Six brush-written characters on the flyleaf: *Notes of the Nine Cauldrons Perfected One*. He opened it. The first line:

"When I was young, people called me the leaky ladle."

Shen Mang snorted out a laugh. A Perfected One, and the first thing he does is call himself a leaky ladle — this old man was fun. He leafed on. It wasn't a method; it was a diary, entry after entry, short as an account book: "Age twelve. Fell into the gorge. At the bottom a fox, tail broken, hungry. Shared half a flatbread with it." "That winter, learned breathing. The goose feather flew every day." A few pages on, a single line by itself: "To cultivate immortality, first cultivate the heart."

Which gorge he had fallen into, where the fox had come from, he couldn't make out; but here was a man who had started writing at twelve and filled eight thick volumes. He slid the first volume back into the case, just as it had been.

That night, after lights out, he lay on his back with the thousand-odd pages of *Normal Human Anatomy* on his stomach. "Haaa —" a long breath out, all of it, and the book sank; in through the nose, and the book slowly rose. On the seventh breath out, his belly sank and, down below came a *pffff* — very quiet. Shen Mang thought: nobody will have noticed. Old Cai couldn't stay still on the top bunk; he shot half his body over the edge, pinching his nose: "Shen Busy, you got a leak?" On the opposite bed Specs went "Hahahaha!" and pounded the bed frame, and only when he'd laughed himself out did he say: "I looked it up. Tao Hongjing was Liang dynasty, Southern Dynasties, not Tang. And Ge Hong isn't five hundred years ago, it's seventeen hundred and some." Shen Mang said, "She got the dynasty wrong. The sentence wasn't wrong."

September the twenty-third, Ma Xiaobao squatted at the edge of the lawn: "Seven people at the retest tomorrow. I bet you come seventh — dead last. A box of protein powder on it: if you're not seventh, the box is yours." He patted Shen Mang's cheek. "If you are seventh, don't bother coming October seventeenth either. Saves me saying that thing for you in front of her."

exits.means: goes to the retest on the twenty-fourth
